The 6:10 Flight
3:15 AM. Every light on the Lakshmi is on. Half the village is on the jetty in their nightclothes, because news travels faster than the ferry.
Three jars of mango pickle. One jar of fish pickle. Two cotton towels. Don't tell me England has towels. I've seen hotel towels. They're thin.
She presses something into your palm. A brass oar-blade, no bigger than a thumb, on a black thread. Your father wore it in every snake-boat race.
Row together or sink together. That was his rule. Find out who rows with you.
Put it on and hug her.
Say nothing. She knows.
"I'll fix the boat, Amma. I promise."
You know about the letter.
She smells of coconut oil and woodsmoke. She doesn't let go for a long time.
Shibu told you. That boy cannot keep a secret in a locked box.
The boat is my job. You do yours.
Shibu drives you to Kochi in his auto, your father's old cricket bag strapped to the roof with a fishing net.
Two hours to the airport. I'll do it in ninety. If we die, we die famous.
Listen. When you're on TV, do one thing for me. Touch your collar. Like this. So I know you're thinking of the auto.
"Collar. Every boundary. Deal."
A secret signal.
"Just drive, Shibu."
Your stomach is upside down.
Saw the news. Congratulations.
Your letter is still in my pocket. On Monday it goes to the league, and a copy goes to your Board.
Unless you want to buy it back. Ten lakh. Think about it on the plane.
Ten lakh to undo one signature. That's more than the boat.
Kochi airport. 5:40 AM. Gate 4. A woman in a denim jacket with a laptop bag and a press lanyard looks up from her coffee, and her eyebrows go all the way up.
Diya Nair. The column you probably hate. You told me "no comment".
I'm on this flight. I cover the World Cup. Which means, for the next six weeks, you can't escape me.
You never answered my question. Now you don't have to.
Same flight. Funny. I was going to ask the Board for your number, and you already gave it to me.
She turns her laptop around. Her column from last week. The headline: "THE NINTH MAN: Who Keeps Dropping Kerala's Best Batter, and Why?"
I never read it. I stopped reading about myself after the fourth time.
"Why do you care?"
Ask her straight.
"You spelt Kuttanad wrong."
Tease her.
Pay for the seat next to hers.
Six hours is a long time.
My brother bowled left-arm for Kozhikode. Dropped four times. He sells insurance now. He says he's happy. He's a good liar.
He was the first one I watched it happen to. You're the second. I want to know who's doing it.
I did not. I spelt it with two Ts. Because I was angry. That's called style.
She laughs. Then she checks the article. Then she very quietly closes the laptop.

Seat 14B. She sleeps for the first hour with her head against the window. Then she wakes up and talks for five straight hours: her brother, the press box, the night she watched your hundred in the rain and nobody else stayed.
You're a terrible person to sit next to. You make me talk.

England. Raining sideways. The team hotel smells of carpet and coffee. Fourteen players in the lobby, and not one of them looks up when you walk in. Except one man. Silver hair, blazer, a Board pin on his lapel.
Prakash Bhandari. Chairman of selectors. Aryan Khurana's uncle.
Let me be clear, so nobody is confused later. You are cover. Aryan has a scan on Thursday.
If he's fit, you fly home on Friday. Don't unpack.
Sameer Pradhan. Captain. Ignore him. He says "don't unpack" to everybody. He said it to me in 2019.
Nets at nine. I watched your hundred on my phone. Bring that.

Midnight. You can't sleep. Walking the corridor, you hear something through the physio room door. A man crying through his teeth. Inside, alone: Aryan Khurana, an ice pack strapped to the back of his thigh.
A syringe box on the table. Painkiller injections.
Get out.
...No. Wait. Shut the door.
It's a tear. Grade two. I can walk. I can't sprint. Thursday I take two of these, I pass the test, and I play.
My uncle has spent six years telling everyone I'm better than you. If I fail on Thursday, he's finished. So am I.
"You'll tear it right through."
Warn him.
"Not my problem."
Six years of being his problem.
You heard nothing tonight. Understand?
Tell the team doctor, and you play the World Cup. Stay quiet, and a man plays on a torn hamstring. Thursday is in two days.
